entities.name: Abu Lu'lu'a
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Abū Luʾluʾa Fīrūz, a Sasanian Persian artisan and slave, etched his name into the annals of early Islamic history not through conquest or statesmanship, but through a singular, momentous act: the assassination of Umar ibn al-Khattab, the second Rashidun Caliph, in November 644 CE. This act of regicide, committed in Medina, profoundly impacted the nascent Islamic empire, triggering a succession crisis and exposing deep-seated tensions within its rapidly expanding dominion. His identity as a non-Arab, formerly enslaved Sasanian, living within the heart of the conquering Arab state, makes his deed a potent symbol of resistance and the complex ethno-religious dynamics of the 7th century Near East.

Fīrūz, originally from Nahavand in Persia, was brought to Medina after the Muslim conquest of the Sasanian Empire, serving as a skilled craftsman. According to historical accounts, his motive stemmed from a grievance over the tax (kharaj) levied upon him by his master, al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, which Umar upheld. On November 3, 644 CE (26 Dhu al-Hijjah 23 AH), Fīrūz ambushed Umar during the Fajr prayer in the Prophet's Mosque, stabbing him six times with a double-bladed dagger. After wounding several others who attempted to apprehend him, Fīrūz either committed suicide or was captured and executed, dying on November 6, 644 CE, three days after Umar succumbed to his wounds.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Abu Lu'lu'a's assassination of Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab directly led to a succession crisis and the election of Uthman, significantly shaping the political trajectory of the early Islamic empire. His act also became a potent symbol of resistance and ethnic tension, resonating through subsequent historical and religious narratives.
